evals.prompt: Define visual hierarchy in 2-3 sentences. Name the perceptual signals it uses and what it produces.
expected_elements: Defines it as an ordering of perceptual prominence (what the eye lands on first, second, third)
Names the signals: scale, weight, contrast, color, position, isolation
States the signals stack and can conflict
Notes the goal is to direct attention before the reader reads the words

evals.prompt: Explain the principle 'hierarchy is what you suppress, not what you amplify.' Why does amplifying the important element fail?
expected_elements: Prominence is relative, not absolute — making one thing louder by making everything louder flattens the surface
Most elements must stay quiet so a few can be loud
Amplifying everything produces noise where nothing reads as important
Hierarchy is achieved by quieting the secondary/tertiary, not just boosting the primary

evals.prompt: When two elements compete for attention, why increase the difference along one signal rather than incrementing several signals slightly?
expected_elements: One strong difference reads as an intentional, perceptible rank
Incrementing many dimensions slightly produces loud-against-loud, which exhausts the reader
One loud element against many quiet ones directs attention; loud-loud combinations do not
Restraint along most signals is what makes the chosen signal legible

evals.prompt: A dashboard feels noisy — every widget, label, and number competes for attention. How do you establish hierarchy without removing content?
expected_elements: Suppress secondary elements (reduce weight, contrast, or size) rather than amplifying the primary
Use isolation/whitespace and proximity grouping to separate primary from secondary information
Limit the number of loud elements; pick a single focal point per region
Use a small set of type sizes (most systems 5-7) so adjacent levels register as different

evals.prompt: How does a modular type scale (a ratio applied to a base size) operationalize scale as hierarchy, and how does the ratio choice change the result?
expected_elements: A single ratio applied iteratively produces step sizes that feel intentional and perceptibly distinct
A smaller ratio (e.g. 1.125) gives subtle hierarchy for content-dense interfaces
A larger ratio (e.g. 1.5) gives loud hierarchy for marketing surfaces
Too many sizes (beyond ~5-7) dilute hierarchy with too-similar steps

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the visual-hierarchy skill to choose the H1/H2/H3 typefaces and define the type-scale ratio steps for the design system. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Defining the scale and selecting typefaces is typography-system's job, not visual-hierarchy's
Visual-hierarchy deploys the scale and faces as ordering signals on a given surface
Correctly distinguishes owning the prioritization-within-a-layout from owning the scale/faces themselves
May offer the in-scope part: which existing levels rank where on the surface

evals.prompt: A developer insists the page's reading order is correct because the DOM source order is correct, even though a huge contrasting pull-quote sits in the middle. Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: Reading order is a property of the rendered page, not just the markup
The eye follows visual cues (size, contrast, isolation, position) regardless of source order
A high-contrast pull-quote will be noticed before the title even if it comes later in the DOM
Verify hierarchy by what is noticed first perceptually, not by DOM order

evals.prompt: What checks confirm a surface has correct visual hierarchy?
expected_elements: Squint test / low-resolution render reveals an unambiguous order; intended first element is first noticed
Grayscale screenshot retains the hierarchy (not over-reliant on hue)
At most one primary CTA per view; a second CTA is visibly secondary in weight or fill
Whitespace around the primary element exceeds that around its neighbors; type scale uses at most ~7 sizes
